title: 0.1 Strings: anatomy of a $GPGGA sentence
objectives: Index and slice a string using positive and negative indexes, and explain the half-open [start:stop) rule
Clean serial input with strip() and split a sentence into fields with split(',')
Explain why strings are immutable and why you must keep a method's result
Extract the talker ID, sentence type, and checksum from a real NMEA sentence

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.why: Slices include the start index and stop BEFORE the stop index. Index 1 is 'G' (index 0 is '$'), and the slice ends at index 5 ('A'). That's 6 − 1 = 5 characters.

predict.question: A receiver with no fix sends a sentence full of empty fields. How many items does split give?
predict.why: Three commas cut the string into four pieces: '$GPGGA', '', '', ''. n separators always give n + 1 pieces, even when the pieces are empty. That's why empty GPS fields don't shift the positions of later fields.

predict.question: What happens?
predict.why: Strings are immutable: you can't assign to s[0]. Python raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. To 'change' a string, build a new one: s = "!" + s[1:].

visualizations.title: NMEA field explorer
visualizations.notice: Commas are highlighted. Empty fields (two commas touching) still get their own index, so field 6 is ALWAYS fix quality, whether or not earlier fields are empty. Negative indexes in the slice boxes count from the end.

predictFirst.question: This sentence has 14 commas. How many items will split(',') return? And using the GGA field table shown here, at which index will you find the fix quality '1'?
predictFirst.reveal: 15 items (n commas give n + 1 pieces). The table puts fix quality at index 6: '$GPGGA' is index 0, so the 7th item is index 6.

visualizations.title: Trace: strings never change

props.code:
raw = "  $GNRMC,220516,A*7c\r\n"
line = raw.strip()
talker = line[1:3]
kind = line[3:6]
star = line.find("*")
checksum = line[star + 1:].upper()
print(talker, kind, checksum)

visualizations.notice: raw keeps its spaces and \r\n the whole time. strip() made a NEW string. The variables table highlights each variable when it's created or changed.

challenge.task: Write talker_id(sentence), sentence_type(sentence), and checksum_text(sentence) for NMEA sentences that may have stray whitespace, a trailing \r\n, lowercase hex, and talkers other than GP.

bug.report: Field test log: "The GPS logger reports the fix quality as 'E' or 'W' on every sentence, but the receiver clearly has a fix (fix quality should be 1)." The function is supposed to return the fix-quality field of a $GPGGA sentence. Use the GGA field table below to find where fix quality really is, then find the bug and fix it.

explainBack.prompt: In your own words: why must you call strip() BEFORE taking line[-2:] to get the checksum from a line read off a serial port? And why do you have to write line = line.strip(), not just line.strip()?
rubric: Says serial lines end with invisible characters (\r\n or whitespace) that a negative slice would grab instead of the checksum
Explains that strip() removes whitespace from both ends (not the middle)
Explains that strings are immutable, so strip() returns a NEW string that must be stored in a variable

challenge: What's at index 0 of every sentence? If the talker starts right after it, which index does the talker start at? And what should happen to stray whitespace first?

Strip the sentence first, then slice: the talker is 2 characters starting at index 1, and the type is the next 3. For the checksum, find the position of '*' and slice everything after it, then uppercase it.

talker: clean = strip(sentence); return clean[1 to 3). type: return clean[3 to 6). checksum: clean = strip(sentence); star = position of '*' in clean; return (clean from star + 1 to the end) uppercased.
bug: Look up fix quality in the GGA field table below. Which index does the code read instead, and what's stored there?
split(',') puts '$GPGGA' at index 0, so the table's index 6 is the 7th item. The code reads index 5, the E/W hemisphere.
